name: SPAC Risks in QC
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Shortcut That Wasn't Free: SPACs and Quantum Computing's Public Debut Wave
lesson.summary: Several quantum computing companies went public through SPAC mergers rather than traditional IPOs, a path that offered speed and lighter scrutiny but carried structural risks, dilution and aggressive projections among them, that have shaped how public markets view these companies today.
lesson.body:
A special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, is a shell company with no underlying business of its own that raises capital through its own IPO and then merges with a private operating company, effectively taking that private company public without the traditional IPO process of an underwritten roadshow. SPACs became extremely popular as a fundraising vehicle across many sectors in 2020 and 2021, and quantum computing was very much part of that wave, with IonQ merging with dMY Technology Group III in 2021 and Rigetti Computing merging with Supernova Partners Acquisition Company II in 2022.

The appeal of this route for quantum computing companies specifically follows directly from the corporate R&D burn rate problem described earlier in this chapter. Pre-revenue, R&D-heavy companies often struggle to meet the demonstrated-revenue and profitability expectations that traditional IPO underwriters and public market investors typically look for. A SPAC merger offered a faster path to public capital markets, with different disclosure norms, at a moment when investor enthusiasm for both SPACs and quantum computing as a theme was unusually strong, letting cash-hungry companies raise substantial capital while that enthusiasm lasted.

That speed came with structural risks that are worth naming specifically. SPAC deals typically involve meaningful dilution from sponsor economics: SPAC sponsors conventionally receive founder shares, often referred to as the promote, equal to roughly 20 percent of the SPAC's outstanding equity, a structure that has drawn criticism and some negotiated modifications over time but that generally dilutes the value ultimately available to the combined company's other shareholders. SPAC deals also carry redemption risk: investors who bought into the original SPAC's IPO are entitled to redeem their shares for cash instead of rolling into the merger, and when redemptions run high, as they often did across many SPAC deals during the broader market downturn of 2022, the merged company can end up with far less actual cash on its balance sheet than the deal's headline size suggested at announcement.

A second, less mechanical risk concerns disclosure. SPAC merger proxy materials have historically been permitted to include forward-looking financial projections with lighter legal liability protections than a traditional IPO prospectus carries, since the safe harbor rules for forward-looking statements applied more broadly to SPAC deals for a period than to traditional IPOs. Critics, and eventually regulators, argued this let a number of SPAC-merged companies across many sectors, quantum computing included, publish ambitious multi-year revenue projections during the merger process that proved considerably too optimistic once the company was actually public and reporting real quarterly results. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission subsequently moved to tighten SPAC-specific disclosure rules in response to concerns of this kind across the broader SPAC market.

Put together, these two structural features, cash raised often coming in below the announced deal size due to redemptions, and early projections set higher than subsequent results supported, help explain why the stock performance of quantum computing's SPAC-merged companies diverged so sharply from their original pitch decks. The next chapter looks at exactly this pattern through the specific, concrete experience of Rigetti Computing, whose financial history illustrates several of these risks converging on a single company.
